# Preface {.unnumbered}

I wrote my undergraduate thesis in Earth Engine as a Geophysics student at Universitas Padjadjaran, in the DRPRS lab. I did not know then that the same few lines of code would follow me for years: to a carbon start-up in Germany, to plantation forests in Riau, to research with partners in Singapore and forestry teams in Brazil, and finally back to a lecture hall at UNSW Sydney.

Each of those places taught me something the tutorials had not. A map can look clean and still be wrong, because the numbers in the image were never understood as physics. A model can score 94 per cent and still fail in the field, because the samples sat next to each other. A client does not want a classifier; they want to know where, how much, and how sure. This book is those lessons, written down in the order I wish I had learned them: first what a sensor actually measures, then the code, then the problems people pay to have solved.

Most of it comes from project work. Some of it comes from the classroom, where I finally had time to ask why the methods I had been using for years actually work. Both are here, side by side, and every chapter ends with something you can run yourself.

## Why this book is free

I studied at UNSW on a scholarship from LPDP, the Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education, paid for by Indonesian taxpayers. I count it as a privilege I owe back. This book is part of repaying it: so that any Indonesian student, officer or engineer, and anyone else who wants it, can learn this work without a scholarship, a course fee or a company account.

The need is real. Indonesia has more than seventeen thousand islands, and many of its hardest problems are spatial: where forest is being lost, which hillsides will slide in the next rain, which neighbourhoods will flood. The satellite data to answer them is free. What is missing is people trained to turn it into decisions, and every geospatial engineer who learns to do this well becomes a multiplier.

## Thank you

At UNSW Sydney, three people supported my learning in remote sensing and GIS: **Professor Samsung Lim**, my supervisor, **Professor Linlin Ge** and **Professor Shawn Laffan**. They gave me their time, their questions and their patience, and they helped a practitioner learn to think like a researcher. This book is, in part, a thank-you to them. What is good in this book owes them a great deal; the mistakes are mine.

## Who this is for

**Environmental scientists, foresters and marine practitioners.** You know the ecosystem. You need the computation to stop being the bottleneck. No programming background is assumed; Chapter [-@sec-javascript] starts from what a variable is.

**GIS professionals moving from desktop to cloud.** Most of what you know transfers. The parts that do not, chiefly the server side execution model, are handled in Chapter [-@sec-server-side] before they can cost you a week.

**Developers and data scientists entering the geospatial domain.** Your coding is not the gap. Part I is where your reading should slow down, because a model trained on physically meaningless features will still report 94 percent accuracy.

**Students and trainers.** Every chapter ends with exercises, and the parts map onto teachable blocks. The [instructor notes](instructor.qmd) suggest course shapes for a five week bootcamp and a three day intensive.

## The route through

| Part | Chapters | You finish able to |
|------|----------|--------------------|
| Principles | P1 to P6 | Explain how optical, thermal and radar sensors form an image, and use the IJB app without code |
| I. Foundations, purpose and physics | 4 chapters | Explain what a pixel measures and choose the right sensor for a question |
| II. The platform | 3 | Write and debug Earth Engine scripts with confidence |
| III. Analysis ready data | 4 | Build composites from optical, radar and terrain sources |
| IV. Feature engineering | 4 | Turn reflectance into ecologically meaningful predictors |
| V. Learning from data | 6 | Explore data, test claims statistically, then train, validate and defend a classification |
| VI. GeoAI and time | 7 | Use foundation-model embeddings, regression, deep learning and time series |
| VII. Hazards | 6 | Map floods, landslides, storms, fire and smoke, and say how sure you are |
| VIII. Food and plantations | 6 | Monitor crops, paddy, land suitability and oil palm, from satellite to drone |
| IX. Forests, carbon and nature | 7 | Track deforestation, carbon, ecosystem services and habitat, and support enforcement |
| X. Mining | 3 | Map mining, its restoration, and its costs and benefits |
| XI. Water and coasts | 3 | Follow the water cycle, map shallow-water depth and mangrove change |
| XII. Solar energy | 4 | Turn sunlight, rooftops and solar farms into a decision |
| XIII. Cities, people and business | 6 | Map urban growth and planning needs (green space, heat, flood exposure), and answer location, transport and economic questions with open data |
| XIV. Communicating results | 4 | Design charts and maps that explain, produce map reports, and ship an app |
| XV. LiDAR: forestry and beyond | 5 | Classify point clouds, find trees, scale plot biomass with GEDI, and map landslide terrain and cities in 3D |
| XVI. Research frontiers | 1 | Start a thesis from a runnable, honest baseline |

: Reading pathways {.striped}

Three shortcuts through the material, depending on why you came.

**The minimum viable analyst.** Chapters [-@sec-physics], [-@sec-ecosystem], [-@sec-optical], [-@sec-cloud], [-@sec-sampling], [-@sec-supervised], [-@sec-accuracy]. From nothing to a validated land cover map with a defensible confusion matrix, in one weekend. This route is written in full.

**The GeoAI sceptic.** Chapters [-@sec-physics], [-@sec-sampling], [-@sec-supervised], [-@sec-embeddings]. Build a classifier the classical way, then rebuild it from satellite embeddings with a fiftieth of the training data, and judge the difference for yourself.

**The person with a deadline.** Chapter [-@sec-apps] first, then work backwards through whatever it depends on.

## How the code works

Every listing is a real file from `scripts/`, generated into the page at build time. Each chapter opens with two buttons: **Open in Code Editor** loads the JavaScript straight into Earth Engine, and **Open in Colab** opens the Python notebook, ready to run. Nothing here is pseudocode and nothing is a fragment that only works in context.

Under each listing is the output that code produced when the book was built: the real maps, charts and tables, not screenshots and not illustrations. That is deliberate. You can check your own run against it, a result is never described that the code did not actually produce, and when a number in the text looks surprising you can see where it came from. Where a chapter needs data that is not in Earth Engine or in a stable public archive, such as a drone image or a frozen timetable, the script downloads the exact files used for the book, so your run can match the printed one. Those [data snapshots](https://github.com/rifkynhsp-byte/Fullstack-Remote-Sensing/releases/tag/data-v1) are listed with their sources and licences.

The comments inside those scripts are the teaching, not decoration. Where a line encodes a decision that could reasonably have gone another way, the comment says which alternatives exist and why this one won. Reading a script top to bottom should feel like sitting beside someone narrating their reasoning.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Running the code
[![Add all book scripts to your Code Editor](https://img.shields.io/badge/Add%20all%20book%20scripts-to%20your%20Code%20Editor-34a853)](https://code.earthengine.google.com/?accept_repo=users/rifkynauvalhsp/Fullstack-Remote-Sensing) &nbsp; One click adds every chapter's script to the Scripts panel of your Earth Engine Code Editor, under *Reader*. Open one and press **Run**. Each chapter also has its own **Open in Code Editor** and **Open in Colab** buttons. A free non commercial account covers every chapter except the export heavy parts of Chapter [-@sec-apps]. Appendix A covers registration and the Python alternative.
:::


## What this site does beyond being a book

Your reading position, chapter progress, quiz scores and notes are kept in your browser and gathered on the [progress dashboard](dashboard.qmd). The **Ask a question** button on every page sends your question to me with the chapter attached; a badly worded question is better than a week stuck.

## Conventions

::: {.callout-note}
## Concept
Background that explains why something works. Skippable on a first pass, worth returning to.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure
A mistake that is easy to make and hard to diagnose. Worth reading even if you skip everything else on the page.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity
A point where technically valid code still produces a scientifically indefensible map.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Something that only shows up in operational work, usually the hard way.
:::

The foundational scripts in Part II descend from the EE101 teaching series by Noel Gorelick, David Gibson, Nicholas Clinton and Hadi, adapted here with gratitude. The mangrove and blue carbon material draws on field data and methodological work from the Indonesian conservation research community, including CIFOR plot data from West Papua. Errors that remain are mine.

## About the author

![](images/author.jpg){.author-photo width="170" fig-alt="Rifky Nauval Hendrawan"}

I'm **Rifky Nauval Hendrawan**, a remote sensing specialist from Indonesia, now living in Sydney. I use satellites, drones and data to help people understand and look after forests, land and the communities that depend on them.

My work has taken me from plantation forests in Riau to carbon projects with a climate start-up in Germany, research with partners in Singapore and forestry teams in Brazil. Today I am a Senior Remote Sensing Specialist at APRIL, and I am finishing a Master of Engineering Science at UNSW Sydney (December 2026).

I wrote this book because the most useful lessons in this field are learned on real projects, often the hard way, and they deserve to be shared freely, in English and in Bahasa Indonesia.

## Work with me

This book is free, and it will stay free. If it has been useful and you need the same methods applied to your own problem, I am open to:

- **Consulting and projects**: satellite and LiDAR analysis, forest inventory and biomass, carbon MRV, land-cover and change mapping, and Earth Engine applications, for companies, NGOs and government.
- **Training**: workshops and courses for teams, in English or Bahasa Indonesia, built on the chapters of this book.
- **Research collaboration and PhD opportunities** in remote sensing, LiDAR, GeoAI and environmental monitoring.
